topics.title: What If Every Hour You Slept Rewound the World?
topics.premise: While you stay awake time moves forward normally, but every hour you sleep rewinds the entire world—and your place in it—backward by one hour while you keep your memories.
topics.world: Present-day Tokyo, Japan, between the 24-hour capsule pods of Shinjuku and the Tokyo Stock Exchange in Kabutocho, a city of missed last trains and commuter micro-naps where a 26-minute nap rewinds the closing bell.

thumbnail.image: You (mustard head, teal scarf) large left of centre jolting awake inside a glowing Shinjuku capsule hotel pod with dark eye bags; a crimson pointer leads to the digital wall clock rolling backward from 'NOV 12' to 'NOV 09' while an empty sleeping-pill blister pack sits by your hand.

topics.rule: As long as you are awake, the clock moves forward at normal speed. The instant you fall asleep or lose consciousness, the entire world—including your physical position and injuries—rewinds by 1 hour for every 1 hour you stay unconscious, while your memory stays intact. Because a human who stays awake 16 hours and sleeps 8 hours only moves forward by 8 net hours (+16 minus 8), you live three subjective days for every one calendar day. The catch: your biological cells still age forward through every rewound day, and if you ever get knocked out or put into a multi-day medical coma, you wake up dragged days backward into the past.
topics.hook: You fall asleep on the 11:40 PM Chuo Line train in Tokyo after bombing the biggest interview of your life, you sleep for eight hours, and when you open your eyes you're sitting right back in the waiting chair at 3:40 PM yesterday with the interviewer calling your name.
beats: Beat 1 — The 3:40 PM Wake-Up Call: You nail the interview on the second try using every answer you heard yesterday, then calculate the math on a paper napkin: 16 hours awake (+16) minus 8 hours asleep (-8) means your life now advances by only 8 net hours a day—giving you three tries at every afternoon.

Beat 2 — Jump 1 (The 26-Minute Shinjuku Nap): You rent a Shinjuku capsule pod 200 meters from the Tokyo Stock Exchange; every day at 3:00 PM you watch which stock spikes at the closing bell, pop into your pod for a 30-minute power nap, wake up at 2:30 PM, and buy the trade before it happens.

Beat 3 — The Panic Insomnia Catch: When your younger sister Hana gets hit by a delivery scooter outside Shinjuku Station, you sprint into a quiet stairwell and squeeze your eyes shut to rewind 15 minutes—only to learn that adrenaline and cortisol spike sleep onset latency, making it physically impossible to fall asleep on command when someone you love is bleeding.

Beat 4 — The Propofol Shortcut: After spending an agonizing 28 minutes trying to fall asleep naturally and having to sleep 45 minutes just to undo the crash, you start carrying high-dose sedatives in your jacket pocket so you can force yourself unconscious in 60 seconds during any emergency.

Beat 5 — Jump 2 (The 3-to-1 Aging Cost & Microsleep Glitches): To stop rewinding every night and reach next month with Hana at normal speed, you push yourself onto a 22-hour-awake schedule—until after 36 hours of sleep debt, involuntary 10-second microsleeps hit your brain in the middle of dinner, making the soup spoon and Hana's sentences stutter backward like a scratched DVD.

Beat 6 — The Midpoint Misconception Breaks: At your annual medical checkup two calendar years later, the doctor stares at your bloodwork in silence: because you have lived three biological days for every one calendar day—plus hundreds of rewound naps—your epigenetic clock and telomeres have aged seven years in twenty-four months.

Beat 7 — The Cost Lands (60%): You vow to quit rewinding and sleep a balanced polyphasic cycle, until Hana's small design shop in Shimokitazawa burns down in an electrical fire **three days ago** while your phone was off on a trip—meaning to reach that Tuesday afternoon and unplug the faulty heater, you have to sleep for 72 net hours backward.

Beat 8 — The 72-Hour Backward Dive: Because the human brain cannot sleep 72 hours straight, you check into a Shinjuku capsule pod and chain-dose sedatives—sleeping 14 hours, waking up for 10 groggy minutes two days ago to swallow another pill, and plunging deeper backward through Thursday, Wednesday, and Tuesday while your breathing slows to the edge of respiratory arrest.

Beat 9 — Jump 3 (The Coma Trap & The Choice at 80%): You wake up on Tuesday afternoon, stagger into Hana's shop, and pull the smoking heater from the wall—but you collapse on the floor from sedative toxicity; as the paramedics load you into the ambulance with an oxygen mask to induce a 48-hour protective coma, you realize that if they put you under for two days, you will rewind past the rescue or never wake up at all.

Beat 10 — Back to You (The Worldview Flip): You rip the IV sedative line from your arm in the ambulance, force yourself to stay awake for 18 straight hours inside the ICU with Hana holding your hand and talking to you through the night so you can finally cross into Wednesday morning—realizing that tomorrow isn't promised by the calendar, it's earned by letting yesterday stay finished.
restarts: Minute 3: Discovering the +16 awake / -8 asleep equation reveals you only advance 8 net hours per day, turning Shinjuku capsule naps into a stock-market time machine.
Minute 6: An accident in front of you reveals the cruel biological catch—panic and adrenaline make it impossible to fall asleep when you need an emergency rewind.
Minute 9: A blood test proves your cells age forward through every rewound day at 3x speed, while sleep deprivation causes reality to glitch backward during microsleeps.
Minute 12: After chain-sleeping 72 hours backward to stop a fire, paramedics try to put you into a medically induced coma that would undo the rescue itself.

content_mine.fact: Homeostatic sleep pressure (Process S, driven by adenosine clearance) prevents a healthy human from sleeping more than 12 to 14 continuous hours once adenosine is cleared, requiring chemical sedation to stay unconscious for 72 hours.

content_mine.fact: Naloxone and flumazenil act as competitive receptor antagonists that can reverse opioid or benzodiazepine sedation within 60 to 120 seconds, forcing an unconscious brain back into waking beta-wave activity.

topics.title: What If Every Bill You Paid Split Across Earth?
topics.premise: Whenever you buy anything, the price is divided equally across all 8.16 billion people on Earth, and you only pay your one-eight-billionth share.
topics.world: Present-day Singapore, between a Chinatown hawker centre and the Marina Bay financial towers, the world's most expensive city for cars and land—where a simple paper permit just to own a car costs $78,000—and Asia's largest currency-clearing hub.

thumbnail.image: You (mustard head, teal scarf) large left of centre tapping a credit card on a glowing Marina Bay real-estate terminal reading '$81,600,000'; a crimson pointer leads to a split-flap receipt printing '$0.01 FROM EVERYONE ON EARTH' while phones in the crowd behind you all light up at once.

topics.rule: Whenever you pay any bill, invoice, or price tag in your own name, the total cost is divided equally across all 8,160,000,000 humans on Earth, deducted instantly in each person's local currency from their bank account, mobile wallet, or physical coin pocket. Any per-person share below half a cent ($0.005—meaning any purchase you make under $40.8 million) rounds down to $0.00 on bank ledgers, costing nobody anything. The catch: you cannot resell anything you buy for cash, and the moment a single purchase crosses $40.8 million, it rounds up to at least 1 full cent pulled simultaneously from every human on the planet.
topics.hook: You're at a Singapore dealership looking at the $78,000 paper permit required just to drive a used sedan to your father's clinic, you accidentally tap your debit card with $14 in the account, and the receipt prints: 'APPROVED — YOUR SHARE: $0.0000095.'
beats: Beat 1 — The $78,000 Permit for Zero Cents: You check your bank app in disbelief—your balance didn't drop by a single cent, and neither did the dealer's or your father's, because $78,000 divided by 8.16 billion people is 0.00095 cents, which bank rounding rules round down to $0.00.

Beat 2 — Jump 1 (The $40.8 Million Free Ceiling): You discover the mathematical sweet spot of ISO 4217 currency rounding: because half a cent ($0.005) times 8.16 billion people equals $40.8 million, any single checkout under $40,799,999 is a completely victimless rounding glitch.

Beat 3 — Salami-Slicing Marina Bay: You buy your parents a $12 million shophouse, charter flights, and clear every patient's bill at your father's dialysis clinic by splitting large invoices into separate sub-$40 million payments so no human on Earth ever loses even 1 cent.

Beat 4 — Crossing the 1-Cent Threshold: A private medical-device conglomerate threatens to shut down the regional supply of dialysis filters unless someone buys the entire $81.6 million factory in a single indivisible escrow transfer by 5:00 PM; you tap your card, crossing the 1-cent floor for the first time.

Beat 5 — Jump 2 (8.16 Billion Phones Ping at Once): At 4:59 PM, every bank account on Earth drops by $0.01 and a single penny vanishes from the pockets of 1.4 billion unbanked adults; in Singapore and New York people laugh at the viral 'One-Cent Ghost,' and emboldened that nobody got hurt, you start making $816 million and $8.16 billion purchases that charge humanity $0.10 and $1.00 a pop.

Beat 6 — The Midpoint Misconception Breaks (The Household & PPP Multiplier): You think charging everyone on Earth $1.00 to build free hospitals in Singapore is harmless—until your father shows you a news feed from rural Malawi and Niger, where average families have 8 children and live on $2.15 a day: your 'harmless' $1.00 per-person charge just pulled $10.00 at once out of a family's tin box, wiping out five days of food.

Beat 7 — The Cost Lands (60%): You realize your power isn't an infinite money glitch—it is an 8.16-billion-person flat poll tax, the most regressive tax in history, where a billionaire in Zurich and a newborn baby in a refugee camp pay the exact same dollar for your choices.

Beat 8 — The Global Clearinghouse Freeze: Because you triggered 5.4 billion simultaneous cross-border micro-debits across 180 currencies, CLS Bank and SWIFT liquidity circuit-breakers slam shut to stop a global bank run, freezing your father's clinic payroll and trapping millions of families without access to their accounts.

Beat 9 — Jump 3 (The Negative-Price Loophole & The Choice at 80%): The Monetary Authority of Singapore traces the origin terminal to your card; if you pay the $81.6 billion emergency liquidity bond to unfreeze the banks, you will extract $10.00 from every poor person on Earth ($80 per large family)—unless you find a market where the price on the invoice is *negative*.

Beat 10 — Back to You (The Worldview Flip): At the commodities desk in Marina Bay, you sign an invoice to take delivery of negatively priced industrial grid surplus and carbon-waste disposal contracts worth -$16.32 billion; because the bill is negative, the terminal divides -$16.32 billion across all 8.16 billion humans—depositing +$2.00 into every single pocket and tin box on Earth—before you cut your card in half.
restarts: Minute 3: Discovering that bank rounding zeroes out any share under $0.005 gives you a $40.8 million ceiling where nobody on Earth pays a cent.
Minute 6: An indivisible $81.6 million factory escrow forces you across the 1-cent threshold, pinging 8.16 billion accounts and coin pockets at the same millisecond.
Minute 9: Seeing how a '$1.00 per human' charge hits an 8-person household living on $2.15/day reveals your power is a devastating global poll tax.
Minute 12: With global currency clearing frozen, you must discover negative-price commodity invoices to turn a global debit into a global payout.
